presenceLabel: Delaware (Lenape) town, raid or claim in this area
presenceNote: Delaware (Lenape) towns were in Ohio (Muskingum, Sandusky) from the 1740s–50s; Kentucky use was seasonal hunting (Henderson 1992) and war parties (1780, 1782). The winter-camps story is shown as c.1750–1775: the start is vague and the end follows Henderson’s “by the 1770s” (low confidence). The 1804 cession is shown as ten Indiana counties, an approximate area.
overlapNote: Shawnee, Mingo, Miami and Wyandot used the same hunting country (Henderson). The 1785 Fort McIntosh land was shared with the Wyandot. The White River claim was derived from the Miami (who disputed it) and the Piankashaw (who disputed the 1804 cession); Art. 5 of the 1804 treaty made the cession void if the Piankashaw would not agree, which the Piankashaw treaty of 27 Aug 1804 then did.
basis: Treaty texts (Fort McIntosh 1785, Greenville 1795, Delaware 1804, Grouseland 1805), Delaware Nation history page, State Dept diplomacy page on Fort Pitt, Wikipedia for Bird 1780 and Bryan Station. Counties for the 1804 cession are an approximation of the treaty line.

eras.label: c.1750–1775 · Winter and hunting camps
eras.text: Forced out of eastern Pennsylvania after the 1737 Walking Purchase, Lenape bands moved into Ohio (Delaware Nation). Henderson (1992): small Shawnee, Mingo, Delaware, Miami and Wyandot hunting camps lay south of the Ohio in the mid-1700s, were moved north after Fort Stanwix, and hunting parties became raiding parties in the 1770s. No Delaware camp site in Kentucky is documented, so none is drawn.

eras.label: 1778–1782 · Fort Pitt, Gnadenhutten, Bryan Station
eras.text: 17 Sept 1778: White Eyes, Killbuck and Captain Pipe signed the Treaty of Fort Pitt. White Eyes died about two months later; Brodhead burned Lenape towns 1779-81; on 8 Mar 1782 militia killed 96 Christian Lenape at Gnadenhutten. Many Lenape then fought with the British; Lenape were at the Aug 1782 Bryan Station siege.

eras.label: 1780 · Bird’s invasion
eras.text: In June 1780 Bird's British and Native force (Shawnee, Odawa, Ojibwe, Delaware, Wyandot and others) came down the Great Miami, went up the Licking and took Ruddle's and Martin's Stations; captives were divided among the nations and many stayed with them until exchanges after Greenville (1795). Route drawn only on the Ohio and Licking reaches.

eras.label: 1785–1795 · Fort McIntosh and Greenville
eras.text: Fort McIntosh (21 Jan 1785) allotted about a third of Ohio to the Wyandot and Delaware; Greenville (3 Aug 1795) ceded the east and south. Both lines are outside Kentucky and drawn thin and dashed.

eras.label: 1804–1805 · White River claim and cession
eras.text: Art. 4 of the 18 Aug 1804 treaty: the United States would treat the Delawares as owners of the country between the White River (north), the Ohio (south), the Greenville line (east) and the Fort Wayne and Vincennes tracts (west). The Miami said they had only allowed the Delawares to occupy it; the Delawares gave the claim up on 21 Aug 1805 at Grouseland. The southern Indiana cession they made in 1804 is shown as ten counties, an approximate area (the Piankashaw said they gave the land to the Delawares “about thirty-seven years ago”, c.1768). The White River claim itself is text only: White River is not on the base map.

properties.kind: county list (cession, general area, outside Kentucky)
properties.note: General area only. Treaty text (Delaware 18 Aug 1804 Art. 1; Piankeshaw 27 Aug 1804 Art. 1): the tract between the Ohio and Wabash rivers, below Clark's Grant, the Vincennes tract and the Vincennes-to-Falls road, the north edge a line parallel to that road and within half a mile of its northernmost bend. Royce's map key (NPS) labels it No. 7, 'in the southern part of the State'. I approximated it by the ten Indiana counties that lie wholly or almost wholly south of a straight Vincennes-Clarksville chord (Crawford, Dubois, Gibson, Harrison, Perry, Pike, Posey, Spencer, Vanderburgh, Warrick; computed from Census county polygons). The real north edge follows the Vincennes road (Buffalo Trace), not county lines, and Clark's Grant (Clark, Floyd, Scott area) is excluded. Edges are county-ragged and low-confidence; a surveyed Royce sheet would replace this.
Main-map extent: the 1804 cession (ten Indiana counties, approximate area), the 1780 route and sourced points.
